outcomes.absoluteFailure:
Among the families who dwell beneath the trees of Rhovanion, certain tales speak of great black wolves drawn by the forest towards places where Men have disturbed its ancient peace. These beasts are said to appear in clearings opened too widely, near trees felled without need, and along paths where Orcs have left signs of destruction. Their enormous size and dark coats would be the marks of a corruption born in the forest's depths. The elders say that these wolves can follow for several nights those who have entered the woods to commit acts of violence, and that their howls echo for an especially long time around places where trees have been burned.

This tradition also attributes a particular influence over Wargs to ancient trees. The oldest oaks and great beeches would retain a strength that these creatures dread, and their roots would protect Men who seek shelter beneath their branches. Some hunters claim that a Warg hesitates to enter a grove left undisturbed for generations, whereas a recently opened clearing attracts packs. Communities familiar with this belief regard their woodland refuges as protected as much by the age of the trees surrounding them as by their distance from the paths. A pack might prowl for a long time along the edge of such a grove, but would eventually abandon its pursuit before the influence of the trees in which the Woodmen place their trust.
outcomes.failure:
The Woodmen know of the great wolves that sometimes accompany Orc-bands along forest paths. Hunters' tales describe them as powerful beasts, able to follow a trail among roots, fallen leaves, and passages choked with branches. Their sense of smell and hearing enables them to recover the movements of a man or animal, while their great size makes them dangerous when they catch their prey. The villages know stories of packs prowling in districts far from habitation, their howls answering one another beneath the trees.

You also know an explanation according to which Wargs derive their coordination from habits acquired while following Orc-bands. Their silent movements and concerted attacks would be the consequences of prolonged training in the woods. The howls they exchange would serve chiefly to gather scattered individuals, like the calls of ordinary wolves. The elders who pass on this interpretation insist that their intelligence remains limited by their hunting instincts. A Warg drawn away from its trail by a fresher scent or the passing of another animal would necessarily abandon its original purpose. Hunters capable of laying several false trails could therefore throw an entire pack into disorder, until its members ended by pursuing different prey.
outcomes.partialSuccess:
The Woodmen know Wargs as great malevolent wolves whose presence sometimes accompanies the Orcs. Their size, strength, and keen senses distinguish them from ordinary predators. They can follow a trail over long distances and pursue travellers through wooded country. Some are powerful enough to carry an Orc warrior, while others range the wild lands in independent packs. Hunters know that these creatures use their sense of smell and hearing to recognise the paths taken by Men, even when visible tracks become difficult to follow.

You also know that Wargs possess an intelligence greater than that of natural wolves. They communicate by howls and growls that express more than the ordinary calls of animals. Several individuals can act together in following a trail or going around an obstacle. The tales handed down in villages speak of their ability to gather and prepare common attacks. Woodmen know the usefulness of trees and high places for observing the movements of these beasts, but also know that a pack can wait beneath a refuge and watch the paths by which Men must eventually descend.
outcomes.success:
The Woodmen's traditions give Wargs a particular place among the malevolent creatures that haunt the forests. Tales passed down by the elders distinguish their intelligence from that of natural wolves and describe their ability to communicate in a language of their own. Wargs can exchange warnings, acknowledge their leaders' decisions, and prepare common enterprises. Their alliance with the Orcs is ancient, and some packs take part in attacks against human settlements. They nevertheless retain their own organisation and can choose their movements independently of their allies.

Hunters familiar with these creatures know the advantages a forest may offer to pursuers. Wargs move swiftly along clear paths, use tracks frequented by animals, and can recognise routes leading to clearings or watering places. Their size makes certain obstacles more difficult to cross, especially tangles of fallen trunks and constricted passages, but their intelligence enables them to seek more favourable ways. Trees offer Woodmen observation posts and refuges beyond the immediate reach of the Wargs' jaws. A pack may nevertheless keep watch on Men sheltering high among the branches and wait until they are forced to move.

The forest tales also stress that Wargs learn to recognise their adversaries' reactions. They can follow an interrupted trail, explore neighbouring passages, and alter their movements when several individuals discover different signs. The cries exchanged beneath the trees help them gather despite the dense vegetation. Woodmen familiar with such behaviour understand that methods effective against a wild animal may fail against a group capable of deliberating and collectively choosing another course of action.
outcomes.absoluteSuccess:
The deepest knowledge of the Woodmen unites their clans' traditions with precise experience of the creatures ranging the forests of Rhovanion. Wargs have the appearance and physical abilities of great wolves, yet their intelligence and language give them a distinct place among wild beings. They acknowledge their own leaders, gather to deliberate, and can plan attacks upon human communities in concert with the Orcs. Their malice goes beyond the necessities of hunting, and their alliances may serve enterprises of destruction or plunder. Some packs nevertheless range the wooded regions on their own account, retaining an organisation independent of armed bands.

Woodmen familiar with their habits know how to interpret the signs of collective movement. Several trails meeting near a passage, renewed tracks around a clearing, or calls exchanged between distant points may reveal a pack watching a territory. Wargs can use their sense of smell to recover a man's movements, but their intelligence also enables them to recognise the routes he might take. A refuge high in the branches protects against their immediate attacks without making them disappear. A pack may wait a long time, explore neighbouring passages, or attempt to prevent fugitives from reaching another tree. Experienced hunters recognise in this behaviour an ability to prepare a common enterprise, rather than a succession of instinctive reactions.

The oldest traditions distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves appearing in tales of the Elder Days. The latter belong to a history bound up with the powers of Morgoth and with evil spirits, whereas Wargs are known above all through their corporeal presence, their language, and their alliances with Orcs. Certain beliefs trace their origin to an ancient corruption of wolves, whose malice was perpetuated through successive generations. The Woodmen pass on these accounts in connection with the changes undergone by the great forests and the appearance of servants of the Shadow. Their knowledge of Wargs nevertheless rests upon observable behaviour: packs communicate, gather, recognise obstacles, and pursue designs of their own.

gmNote: GM verification: absolute failure — supernatural protection attributed to old trees; failure — intelligence reduced to instinct and an alleged universal vulnerability to false trails; successful results — organisation, language, and woodland knowledge. The belief concerning trees is a tradition proposed for MERP-UI.
